title: THE TORAH FORBADE A MAN FROM TAKING A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER — BUT THE DEEPER REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE
paragraphs: THE TORAH FORBADE A MAN FROM TAKING A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER — BUT THE DEEPER REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE

Leviticus 18:17 was never merely an ancient restriction about forbidden relationships. Buried inside its Hebrew words is a warning about desire, boundaries, family, holiness—and why grace never means God stopped caring about what sin destroys.
There are verses in the Bible we underline because they comfort us.
There are verses we memorize because they strengthen us.
And then there are verses we quietly move past because they make us uncomfortable.
Leviticus 18:17 is one of them.
It speaks about sex.
Family.
Boundaries.
Desire.
And a form of sexual transgression that God describes with startling severity.
But stay with me.
Because if you read this only as an ancient prohibition concerning somebody else's scandal, you may completely miss the mirror hidden inside it.
The verse says:
עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿervat ishah u-vittah lo tegalleh.
Literally, the opening thought is:
“The nakedness of a woman and her daughter you shall not uncover.”
The verse continues by prohibiting taking her son's daughter or daughter's daughter for the purpose of uncovering nakedness, explaining that they are close relatives.
Then comes a devastating Hebrew word:
זִמָּה — zimmah.
The term carries the sense of wickedness, depravity, or an outrageous sexual offense.
God was not merely regulating ancient household arrangements.
He was drawing a boundary.
A man could not sexually possess a woman and then cross into her daughter.
Nor could desire simply continue downward into the woman's granddaughter.
There was a line.
And God said:
Do not cross it.
Why?
Because people are not collections of bodies for someone else's appetite.
Families are not hunting grounds for uncontrolled desire.
Sexual desire was never intended to become a god that decides for itself what it may consume.
And perhaps that is where this ancient command suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because we live in a culture that has learned how to rename almost everything except the damage it leaves behind.
We call lust “chemistry.”
We call secrecy “privacy.”
We call compromise “following your heart.”
We call pornography “entertainment.”
We call emotional adultery “just talking.”
We call boundaries “repression.”
We call conviction “judgment.”
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, the human heart learns one of the oldest lies ever whispered:
If I desire it strongly enough, perhaps I am entitled to it.
But Scripture refuses that lie.
Leviticus 18 begins with God telling Israel that they were not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
In other words:
God's people were not permitted to obtain their sexual ethics simply by looking around at what everybody else was doing.
That should stop us.
Because neither are we.
Popular does not automatically mean holy.
Legal does not automatically mean righteous.
Consensual does not answer every moral question Scripture asks.
Desirable does not mean permissible.
And feeling something deeply does not automatically transform that desire into God's will.
There are boundaries God establishes precisely because He sees farther than our appetites can see.
Sin usually shows us the moment.
God sees the aftermath.
Sin shows the pleasure.
God sees the person.
Sin says, Take.
God asks, What will this taking destroy?
That is why Leviticus 18:17 matters.
But there is another danger here.
We can read a passage describing sexual sin and immediately begin thinking about somebody else.
Someone else's affair.
Someone else's pornography.
Someone else's broken marriage.
Someone else's sexual history.
Someone else's scandal.
Someone else's secret.
And suddenly Scripture becomes binoculars when God intended it to become a mirror.
Maybe you have never committed the specific offense described in Leviticus 18:17.
But have you ever allowed desire to overrule obedience?
Have you ever secretly entertained what you publicly condemn?
Have you ever looked at someone as an object instead of a person bearing God's image?
Have you ever hidden messages because you knew they would wound your spouse?
Have you ever deleted a conversation because daylight would expose what darkness made easier?
Have you ever returned to pornography after promising God it was the last time?
Have you ever crossed an emotional boundary and defended yourself because “nothing physical happened”?
Have you ever wanted something God said no to—and quietly resented Him for saying no?
Now the room gets quieter.
Because suddenly this is not merely about those people.
It is about the human heart.
Mine.
Yours.
Ours.
And this is precisely where Christianity becomes radically different from moral performance.
The Gospel does not say good people stand on one side while disgusting people stand on the other.
The Gospel says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
Every one of us eventually arrives before God without enough righteousness of our own to save ourselves.
Religious people need Jesus.
Sexually broken people need Jesus.
Adulterers need Jesus.
Pornography addicts need Jesus.
People carrying secret fantasies need Jesus.
People whose marriages have collapsed need Jesus.
People who crossed boundaries years ago and still wake up ashamed need Jesus.
People who were sinned against need Jesus.
And people who did the sinning need Jesus.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross.
This is where grace is often misunderstood.
Grace is not God looking at evil and saying:
“It doesn't matter.”
Look at Calvary.
Grace says it mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
Jesus did not die to convince God that sin was harmless.
Jesus bore sin.
The cross simultaneously destroys our excuses and destroys our hopelessness.
You cannot stand beneath the cross and honestly say sin doesn't matter.
But neither can the repentant sinner stand beneath the cross and say redemption is impossible.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy God does not lower His holiness to rescue sinners.
He comes for sinners Himself.
Jesus touches people respectable religion preferred to avoid.
He receives the disgraced.
He confronts hypocrites.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
But notice carefully:
Jesus never needed to redefine darkness as light in order to love people trapped in darkness.
That is something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Truth without grace can become cruelty.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
But in Jesus Christ we encounter both.
John writes that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Perhaps your scandal isn't public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your family doesn't know.
Your church doesn't know.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Your browser history knows.
Your deleted messages know.
Your memories know.
And God knows.
That last sentence may frighten you.
But keep reading.
Because the God who knows is also the God who calls sinners home.
You do not have to clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to receive a genuinely repentant sinner.
You come into the light.
You confess.
You repent.
You stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what Christianity offers.
Not merely concealment.
Cleansing.
Not merely reputation management.
Forgiveness.
Not merely behavior modification.
New life.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door out of the prison you kept calling freedom.
Somebody needs to read that twice.
You have been protecting the very thing that has been poisoning you.
Protecting the conversation.
Protecting the relationship.
Protecting the addiction.
Protecting the secret account.
Protecting the fantasy.
Protecting the bitterness.
Protecting the excuse.
Protecting the hidden version of yourself.
And wondering why you cannot breathe spiritually.
Maybe freedom begins when you stop asking God to bless what He has been asking you to bury.
Leviticus says there are boundaries.
Jesus shows us what happens when boundary-breakers come home.
He does not tell the repentant sinner that holiness no longer matters.
He gives sinners something infinitely better:
mercy that leads them toward holiness.
The Gospel is not:
“Stay exactly as you are because nothing matters.”
Neither is it:
“Fix yourself, and perhaps God will love you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Then the risen Christ calls us to follow Him.
Grace meets us in the wreckage.
Grace does not leave us there.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Your affair does not have to be your final identity.
Your addiction does not have to write the ending.
Your sexual past does not have sovereign authority over your future.
Your hidden sin does not have to remain hidden until it destroys everything.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
But there is something you must understand.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending consequences never existed.
Some wounds require confession.
Some relationships require boundaries.
Some marriages require patient rebuilding.
Some patterns require accountability.
Some crimes require justice.
Some damage cannot be repaired overnight.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
Grace gives us courage to finally face truth without running away from God.
And if you were the one violated, manipulated, exploited, or betrayed, hear this carefully:
another person's sin is not permission for Christians to bury your pain under religious clichés.
God's commands concerning sexual boundaries reveal that sexual wrongdoing matters.
People matter.
Bodies matter.
Families matter.
Faithfulness matters.
What was done in darkness matters.
And Christ's compassion for wounded people matters.
This is why the church must become a place where holiness and mercy meet.
Where predators cannot hide behind religious language.
Where victims are heard.
Where repentant sinners can confess without being told their sin was harmless.
Where broken people can seek help without becoming entertainment for gossip.
Where accountability is real.
Where forgiveness is preached.
Where restoration is pursued wisely.
Where Jesus—not shame, lust, reputation, or scandal—has the final authority.
Maybe you came into this article expecting an unusual Old Testament law.
Instead, Scripture found you.
If something inside you has been whispering while you read this—
This is me.
Do not silence it.
Bring it to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret conversation.
Not after one more video.
Not after one more meeting.
Not after one more compromise.
Today.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
Ask Him for mercy.
Turn from what you know is sin.
And where necessary, seek mature, trustworthy Christian accountability and appropriate professional or pastoral help.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need freedom.
And freedom has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Not because strangers need the details of your private struggle—you do not owe the internet your intimate confession—but because sometimes three simple words become a stake driven into the ground:
I don't want darkness controlling me anymore.
Your testimony may become the sentence another broken believer needed to survive tonight.
And if someone came to mind while reading this, don't weaponize the article against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Then, if appropriate, send it privately and say, “I thought we both needed this.”
You may need these words on a night when temptation sounds reasonable again.
We glorify God by trusting and obeying Christ; financial support should flow freely from gratitude and conviction, never spiritual pressure.
Not because clicking “Share” makes someone righteous.
Only Christ saves.
Perhaps somebody is losing a battle nobody knows they're fighting.
Perhaps someone believes their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
And perhaps God will use the truth you were willing to pass along to remind them that there is still a road home.
Leviticus 18 reminds us that God draws boundaries around what is holy.
The cross reminds us what it cost to redeem those who crossed His boundaries.
And the empty tomb reminds us that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
So stop running.
Stop editing the story.
Stop hiding the evidence from everyone while pretending you can hide your heart from God.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy.
Then get up and follow Jesus.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about your story will not be what you did in the darkness.
Perhaps the most shocking thing will be what Jesus did after you finally stepped into the light.
Your scandal may explain the chapter—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
